articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for Iraq Development Bank Wind-Down
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran General License FF-1, replacing the previous General License FF.

This amended license authorizes transactions that are ordinarily incident and necessary to wind down dealings involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, also known as Iraq Development Bank, and any entities it owns 50 percent or more.
The wind-down period for these transactions is authorized through 12:01 a.m. Eastern Standard Time on December 1, 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Designations Targeting North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities and individuals related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, and the reasons for their designation, are expected to be released in accompanying enforcement information or press releases.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to counter threats posed by these regions through economic sanctions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to a $1,529,685 settlement with OFAC for nine apparent violations of Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services from the U.S. to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA). MMZA was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company, JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, making it a blocked person by operation of law, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List until June 2022.

OFAC determined that the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement amount reflects these factors. This case highlights the importance of thorough sanctions diligence, especially in acquisitions and oversight of foreign operations, to identify blocked entities through ownership structures.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting Requirements
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has amended 11 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.

These revisions, part of OFAC's ongoing review to keep guidance current, address topics such as jurisdictions subject to U.S. sanctions, blocking and rejecting funds transfers, interest on blocked funds, service charges, and notification to customers when property is blocked.

The updated FAQs also clarify reporting procedures for blocked property and rejected transactions, including the required format for Annual Reports of Blocked Property and distinguishing customer inquiries from payment instructions. Initial blocking and rejected-transaction reports are generally due within 10 business days.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.
Additionally, OFAC issued new general licenses pertaining to Iran and Russia, and amended several Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance on these changes.
These actions reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions policy, with both new restrictions and targeted relief being implemented across various programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA).

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, 'Transactions Authorized Pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations,' and PAIPA General License 2, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Certain Entities Blocked on October 19, 2026.'
These actions aim to protect American intellectual property by targeting entities involved in illicit activities, while providing clear guidance for authorized wind-down transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and an updated Frequently Asked Question.
These updates aim to provide clarity and adjust existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Venezuela.
Specific details of the amendments and the updated FAQ are available on the OFAC website, impacting entities and individuals engaged in Venezuela-related activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation.

In conjunction with these actions, OFAC issued new and amended general licenses, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions, to provide guidance on the scope of the new restrictions and authorized activities.
These measures reflect the U.S. government's continued efforts to exert pressure on these regimes and address perceived threats to national security and foreign policy.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation.
This action signifies a targeted adjustment to the existing sanctions regime concerning Venezuela.
Further details regarding the entity or individual whose designation has been removed are available on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.
These designations aim to disrupt the financial networks and operations of those engaged in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing globally.
The action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating these threats through the use of financial sanctions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Fined $1,529,685 by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of OFAC's Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations occurred between September 2018 and March 2022, when Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer that was majority-owned by a designated entity.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, emphasizing the importance of robust due diligence, especially when dealing with entities that may be indirectly owned by sanctioned parties.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 Over Multiple Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of various OFAC sanctions programs, including those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations stemmed from the bank processing payments involving blocked banks, failing to prioritize alerts for customers matching blocked persons, not promptly updating watchlists, and mishandling accounts associated with blocked persons due to human error.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. This settlement was part of a larger, coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based logistics company, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC's counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations.

The violations occurred when Pegasus arranged for the shipment of equipment from a designated supplier in China and failed to identify the equipment as such due to deficiencies in its compliance program. Pegasus also initially failed to respond fully to an OFAC administrative subpoena.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, but noted Pegasus' extensive remedial measures. This case highlights the sanctions risks for logistics and freight forwarding companies, particularly regarding dealings in blocked property.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent sanctions violations.
The details of the specific violations leading to this significant penalty were not immediately disclosed in the summary information.
This enforcement action underscores OFAC's commitment to holding individuals accountable for breaches of U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $60,764
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has reached a settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to pay $60,764 for apparent sanctions violations.
The specific nature of the violations leading to this settlement was not detailed in the initial announcement.
This action serves as a reminder for companies across various sectors to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Fined $1,050,000 by OFAC for Russia-Related Sanctions Violations
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a global advisory firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle its potential civil liability with OFAC.

The violations involved indirectly dealing in the prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, an entity on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification (SSI) List. FTI Consulting issued invoices whose ultimate obligor was VTB and continued work even as those invoices went unpaid beyond the permissible tenor.
OFAC classified the apparent violations as non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement amount was aggravated above the schedule to promote future compliance.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Pays $275 Million OFAC Penalty for Iran Sanctions Evasion
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle its potential civil liability for 32 apparent violations of OFAC's Iran sanctions regulations.

Between November 2023 and June 2025, AEL purchased liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) shipments from a Dubai-based trader, which were disguised as Omani and Iraqi origin but actually originated from Iran. AEL caused U.S. financial institutions to process 32 USD-denominated payments totaling approximately $192.1 million for these shipments.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, citing AEL's reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions and the substantial harm caused to Iran sanctions objectives.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities Fined $1,110,661 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a Florida-headquartered brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to OFAC to settle its potential civil liability for 481 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs.

For nearly a year, from June 2021 to June 2022, TradeStation provided investment services to customers located in Iran, Syria, and the Crimea region of Ukraine, enabling them to execute securities-related transactions.

The violations stemmed from compliance control failures, including issues with geo-blocking software and a lapse in internal oversight. OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, with the settlement reflecting significant remedial measures taken by TradeStation.

articles.headline: Individual Receives $3,777,000 OFAC Penalty for Egregious Sanctions Violation
body: An individual has been assessed a substantial civil penalty of $3,777,000 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for an apparent sanctions violation.
The penalty amount, which is ten times the statutory IEEPA base amount, indicates that OFAC considered the circumstances of the violation to be egregious.

Further details regarding the specific nature of the violation and the individual involved were not immediately released, but the significant fine highlights OFAC's strict enforcement posture against serious breaches of sanctions law.

articles.headline: IMG Academy Fined $1,720,000 by OFAC for Counternarcotics Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, a Bradenton, Florida-based school and athletic training facility, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC's counternarcotics sanctions.

Over five consecutive years, IMG Academy repeatedly transacted with two individuals sanctioned by OFAC due to their ties to a Mexican-based drug cartel. The school accepted tuition payments from these individuals for the enrollment of their children.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, but acknowledged IMG Academy's substantial cooperation and remedial measures. This case emphasizes the importance for academic institutions to implement effective, risk-based controls to prevent sanctions violations.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Major Penalty Against Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting significant penalties and orders against several financial institutions and individuals.

A notable action includes a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, National Association, for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. This penalty was part of a coordinated enforcement action with FinCEN and OFAC.

Other actions include a cease and desist order and civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for BSA compliance program deficiencies, and orders of prohibition against individuals for embezzlement.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
